newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. officer acquitted, chaos in Bronx courtroom.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. officer acquitted, chaos in Bronx courtroom.

text.p: A New York City police officer accused of choking a man to death in a dispute over touch football on a Bronx street was cleared of homicide charges Monday, sparking a chaotic, angry scene at the courthouse.

The emotional three-week trial ended with New York Supreme Court Judge Gerald Sheindlin deciding that the prosecution had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that officer Francis Livoti, 37, was guilty of criminally negligent homicide in the death of 29-year-old Anthony Baez in December 1994.

"I do not find the defendant is innocent," Sheindlin said. "I do find, based on the quality of the evidence presented, that the people failed to establish guilt of the defendant beyond reasonable doubt."

As the judge finished reading his decision in the trial, which Livoti had requested be heard without a jury and decided by the judge, relatives of Baez broke down in tears and supporters threw newspapers across the courtroom shouting, "So, a killer is going to walk free" and "Murderer, murderer."

Court officers quickly ushered the judge off the bench and Livoti was escorted out of the courtroom by members of the police union. Outside the Supreme Court in the Bronx, hundreds of people protested the decision before dispersing.

Baez was playing touch football with his four brothers on the street outside his family's home in the early hours of Dec. 22 when the ball hit Livoti's parked police car several times. Authorities said Livoti ordered the brothers to stop playing or go to the park.

When they refused, Livoti arrested the youngest brother, David Baez. It was then that a confrontation between Anthony Baez and the officer began. In the scuffle Baez was alleged to have shoved Livoti, refusing to be handcuffed behind his back.

Five police officers testified that Baez put up such a fierce struggle it was difficult for them to subdue and handcuff him. All the officers denied that they or Livoti used a choke hold on Baez, who died on the Bronx street.

The city medical examiner and a nationally prominent asthma expert testified that Baez died of asphyxia when his neck and chest were compressed, but the defence argued that Baez died from a pre-existing asthma condition.
Livoti did not testify during his trial.
The judge called the death "tragic, unecessary and avoidable" and said Livoti's conduct "failed to rise to the level one would expect of a professional."
A $48 million civil suit against the officer and the city is pending. U.S. Attorney Mary Jo White said she would review the evidence to determine whether federal criminal charges should be filed.
Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who called the judge's decision "careful" and "conscientious," said the officer will face disciplinary proceedings within the police department.

Bronx Borough President Fernando Ferrer said the verdict was "a setback for our city" and called on the police department to enforce its rules against brutality, reports of which have increased in recent years at the same time that crime statistics are falling.
